headline: High: shared filesystem and shell/write capabilities create prompt-injection, leakage, and cascading-action risks; ECC’s self-isolation does not fully separate it from slim’s container workspace.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: ECC reads/writes local files and uses MCP, while slim reads/writes filesystem artifacts and runs interactive commands. If they share a workspace or files are passed between them, attacker-controlled content from one can be treated as instructions by the other. ECC’s self-isolation helps only within its own boundary; slim has no comparable provenance guard.
conditions: IF both agents are pointed at the same directory or file tree, prompt injection becomes plausible.
IF either agent parses the other’s file output as instructions, the risk materializes.
mitigations: Separate working directories for each agent.
Disable automatic instruction parsing from files.
Require manual review before copying outputs between agents.
Use provenance tags on shared artifacts.
requires-engineering: add content-sanitization or trust-boundary enforcement.

B_data_leakage.rationale: ECC touches session summaries, hooks, MCP configs, and security findings; slim touches container images, certificate private keys, environment variables, and registry credentials. If they share a workspace or logs, sensitive material can move from one agent’s files into the other’s outputs. ECC’s allowlisted egress and slim’s broad egress do not prevent local file exposure.
conditions: IF both agents can read the same filesystem artifacts, leakage is possible.
IF either agent exports its context into logs or reports, sensitive data can be exposed.
mitigations: Keep secrets in separate directories.
Redact private keys and credentials before handoff.
Restrict log retention to minimal necessary data.
Run each agent under distinct OS users.
requires-engineering: enforce per-agent workspace ACLs.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: ECC can write the filesystem, modify git state, and use MCP; slim can also write the filesystem and execute shell commands. On a shared directory, concurrent writes and command-driven mutations can collide, and ECC’s session-state files plus slim’s container artifacts make overwrite risk concrete. No locking mechanism is documented for the pair.
conditions: IF both agents operate on the same git checkout or output directory, write conflicts can occur.
IF either agent runs without external locking, last-writer-wins corruption is plausible.
mitigations: Use separate output directories.
Pause one agent before the other writes.
Avoid shared git branches for concurrent edits.
Snapshot the workspace before each run.
requires-engineering: add file locks or transactional writes.

D_cascading_error.rationale: ECC produces session summaries, learned skills, and security findings; slim consumes interactive CLI input and can act on filesystem artifacts. If slim treats ECC’s generated text as authoritative, errors can cascade into incorrect container changes or analysis outputs. ECC’s subagent model does not verify slim’s downstream actions by default.
conditions: IF slim uses ECC-generated summaries as ground truth, cascading error is possible.
IF ECC outputs are copied into slim prompts without verification, downstream mistakes can propagate.
mitigations: Require independent verification of ECC outputs.
Mark generated summaries as untrusted.
Use a checklist before acting on agent-produced facts.
Limit slim to read-only analysis when fed ECC output.
requires-engineering: add validation gates between agents.

E_compliance.rationale: ECC handles session summaries, hooks, and security findings; slim handles container images, certificate private keys, and registry credentials. The profiles do not show a direct residency or certification mismatch, so only a limited compliance concern is visible: if regulated secrets are shared across their logs or workspaces, retention and access controls may diverge. Both agents are cited because the mismatch would arise from their combined handling.
conditions: IF regulated secrets are stored in shared logs or artifacts, retention mismatch becomes relevant.
IF one agent’s workspace is subject to stricter deletion rules than the other’s, compliance gaps appear.
mitigations: Keep regulated data out of shared artifacts.
Set short log-retention windows.
Separate access controls by agent.
Review data-handling policies before joint runs.
requires-engineering: align retention and deletion workflows.
